stem: According to the Sepsis-3 consensus, how is sepsis defined?

options.A: Infection with hypotension responsive to fluids
options.B: Bacteraemia with fever above 38.3 °C
options.C: Life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection (acute SOFA rise ≥2)
options.D: Two or more SIRS criteria in the presence of suspected or confirmed infection, with or without organ dysfunction
options.E: Infection with a lactate above 4 mmol/L

explanation: Sepsis-3 abandoned SIRS-based definitions and "severe sepsis". Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction due to a dysregulated host response to infection, identified clinically by an acute change in total SOFA score of 2 points or more, which is associated with in-hospital mortality of about 10%. SOFA-2 note: a revised score, SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025), keeps six organ systems (renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis), updates the organ-support drugs and devices used for scoring, revises several thresholds and adds alternative variables when measurements are unavailable; it predicted ICU mortality slightly better (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.77). Sepsis-3 is defined with the original SOFA score, so this calculation uses the original SOFA.
referenceText: Singer et al. 2016 (Sepsis-3) [198]; SOFA-2, JAMA 2025 [250]
updateNote: SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025) note added; calculation uses original SOFA, as Sepsis-3 requires.

stem: Which criteria identify septic shock according to Sepsis-3?

options.A: Lactate above 4 mmol/L regardless of blood pressure
options.B: MAP below 65 mmHg that responds to a 30 mL/kg fluid bolus
options.C: Vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 mmHg and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids
options.D: Systolic BP below 90 mmHg on two readings
options.E: Need for any vasopressor dose in a patient with positive blood cultures and fever

explanation: Sepsis-3 defines septic shock as a subset of sepsis with profound circulatory, cellular and metabolic abnormalities: persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 mmHg and serum lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume resuscitation. Hospital mortality exceeds 40%.
referenceText: Singer et al. 2016 (Sepsis-3) [198]

stem: What do the Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (2021, reaffirmed 2026) recommend regarding qSOFA?

options.A: It is the preferred single screening tool on hospital wards and in the emergency department
options.B: It is only valid in patients over 65 years
options.C: It replaces the SOFA score in the ICU
options.D: It should not be used as a single screening tool, compared with SIRS, NEWS or MEWS
options.E: It is required to diagnose sepsis

explanation: qSOFA (respiratory rate ≥22/min, altered mentation, systolic BP ≤100 mmHg) is specific but insensitive for sepsis. SSC 2021 recommends against using it as a single screening tool; SIRS, NEWS or MEWS are more sensitive. qSOFA identifies patients at higher risk of death. SSC 2026 again recommends NEWS, NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS over qSOFA as a single screening tool (strong recommendation, moderate certainty). SOFA-2 note: a revised score, SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025), keeps six organ systems (renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis), updates the organ-support drugs and devices used for scoring, revises several thresholds and adds alternative variables when measurements are unavailable; it predicted ICU mortality slightly better (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.77). Sepsis-3 is defined with the original SOFA score, so this calculation uses the original SOFA.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Singer et al. 2016 (Sepsis-3) [198]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]; SOFA-2, JAMA 2025 [250]
updateNote: Reaffirmed in SSC 2026 (strong, moderate); SOFA-2 note added.

stem: A septic patient's platelet count falls from 220 × 10⁹/L to 45 × 10⁹/L. What is the SOFA coagulation subscore at this platelet count?
explanation: SOFA coagulation points: platelets below 150 = 1, below 100 = 2, below 50 = 3, below 20 = 4 (all × 10⁹/L). A count of 45 × 10⁹/L therefore scores 3 points, representing a rise of 3 points from baseline. SOFA-2 note: a revised score, SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025), keeps six organ systems (renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis), updates the organ-support drugs and devices used for scoring, revises several thresholds and adds alternative variables when measurements are unavailable; it predicted ICU mortality slightly better (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.77). Sepsis-3 is defined with the original SOFA score, so this calculation uses the original SOFA.
referenceText: Vincent et al. 1996 (SOFA score) [229]; SOFA-2, JAMA 2025 [250]
updateNote: SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025) note added; calculation uses original SOFA, as Sepsis-3 requires.

stem: A ventilated patient with pneumonia has a PaO2/FiO2 ratio of 180 mmHg. What is the respiratory SOFA subscore?
explanation: Respiratory SOFA: PaO2/FiO2 below 400 = 1, below 300 = 2, below 200 with respiratory support = 3, below 100 with respiratory support = 4. A ratio of 180 on mechanical ventilation scores 3. SOFA-2 note: a revised score, SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025), keeps six organ systems (renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis), updates the organ-support drugs and devices used for scoring, revises several thresholds and adds alternative variables when measurements are unavailable; it predicted ICU mortality slightly better (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.77). Sepsis-3 is defined with the original SOFA score, so this calculation uses the original SOFA.
referenceText: Vincent et al. 1996 (SOFA score) [229]; SOFA-2, JAMA 2025 [250]
updateNote: SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025) note added; calculation uses original SOFA, as Sepsis-3 requires.

stem: For an adult with probable septic shock, what is the recommended time frame for starting antimicrobials?

options.A: Within 6 hours to allow complete diagnostic work-up
options.B: Within 24 hours once source is identified
options.C: Within 3 hours of recognition in all cases
options.D: After blood culture results are available
options.E: Immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition

explanation: SSC 2026 recommends antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour, for septic shock and for probable or definite sepsis without shock (strong, very low certainty). For possible sepsis without shock, a rapid assessment is suggested, with antimicrobials within 3 hours if concern for infection persists.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026 wording of the 1-hour antimicrobial recommendation.

stem: A ward patient has possible sepsis without shock; the diagnosis is uncertain after initial review. What does SSC 2021 suggest?

options.A: Withhold antimicrobials until cultures are positive
options.B: Rapid assessment, then antimicrobials within 3 hours if concern for infection persists
options.C: Observe for 24 hours before deciding
options.D: Start antifungal therapy empirically
options.E: Give broad-spectrum antimicrobials within 1 hour, regardless of the diagnostic uncertainty

explanation: To balance harm from unnecessary antibiotics against delays, SSC 2021 suggests a time-limited course of rapid investigation for patients with possible sepsis without shock, and administering antimicrobials within 3 hours from recognition if concern for infection persists. SSC 2026 retains this time-limited approach for possible sepsis without shock (conditional, very low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with suspected septic shock needs antibiotics. What is the recommended approach to blood cultures?

options.A: Antibiotics must always wait until two full sets of blood cultures have been obtained
options.B: Obtain cultures before antimicrobials if this does not substantially delay therapy
options.C: Cultures are unnecessary in septic shock
options.D: Only one set of cultures from a central line is required
options.E: Cultures should be taken 24 hours after starting antibiotics

explanation: Appropriate cultures, including at least two sets of blood cultures (aerobic and anaerobic), should be obtained before starting antimicrobials when this causes no substantial delay (e.g. under 45 minutes). Antimicrobials quickly sterilise cultures and reduce yield. SSC 2026 recommends collecting blood cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials (strong, low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: For a patient with sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, what initial crystalloid volume does SSC 2021 suggest?

options.A: 10 mL/kg within 6 hours
options.B: No fixed volume; vasopressors first
options.C: 1 L total, followed by vasopressors
options.D: At least 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours
options.E: 50 mL/kg within the first hour

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours (weak recommendation), followed by fluid administration guided by dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness, capillary refill time and lactate. The volume should be individualised in heart failure or end-stage kidney disease. SSC 2026 retains the suggestion of at least 30 mL/kg in the first 3 hours (conditional, low certainty), individualised and frequently reassessed, and suggests dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness over examination or static measures alone.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: What is the initial mean arterial pressure target recommended for adults with septic shock on vasopressors?

options.A: 55 mmHg
options.B: 65 mmHg
options.C: 75 mmHg
options.D: 85 mmHg
options.E: 90 mmHg

explanation: SSC 2026 recommends an initial MAP target of 65 mmHg over higher targets (strong, moderate certainty), managed as a range (for example within 5 mmHg), and suggests an initial MAP range of 60–65 mmHg for adults aged 65 years or older (conditional, low certainty). In the 65 trial, permissive hypotension (MAP 60–65) in older patients reduced vasopressor exposure without increasing mortality. Higher targets increase arrhythmias.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Lamontagne et al. 2020 (65 trial) [124]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026: MAP 65 mmHg as a range; 60–65 mmHg if aged ≥65 years.

stem: How does SSC 2021 suggest using lactate in septic shock?

options.A: Lactate above 2 mmol/L mandates a further 30 mL/kg fluid bolus each time it is measured
options.B: Lactate is not useful and should not be measured
options.C: Lactate must be normal before vasopressors are started
options.D: Guide resuscitation to lower elevated lactate, alongside other perfusion measures
options.E: Use lactate clearance alone to decide on antibiotics

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests guiding resuscitation to decrease serum lactate in patients with elevated lactate, recognising that lactate is not a direct measure of tissue perfusion and can be raised by beta-2 stimulation, liver dysfunction and thiamine deficiency. SSC 2026 suggests serial lactate measurement to guide resuscitation (conditional, low certainty), with fluids individualised after the initial bolus rather than aiming to normalise lactate.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: When does SSC 2021 suggest starting IV hydrocortisone in septic shock?

options.A: Ongoing noradrenaline or adrenaline ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for at least 4 hours
options.B: Only when vasopressin has failed
options.C: Only if a random cortisol is below 400 nmol/L
options.D: Only after a short ACTH stimulation test shows an inadequate cortisol response
options.E: In all patients with sepsis at presentation

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (e.g. 50 mg every 6 hours) for adults with septic shock and an ongoing vasopressor requirement of at least 0.25 µg/kg/min for 4 hours or more. ACTH testing is not needed to guide treatment. SSC 2026 continues to suggest IV corticosteroids for adults with septic shock (conditional, low certainty); the ≥0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥4 hours starting criterion comes from SSC 2021.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: How did the ADRENAL and APROCCHSS trials differ in their findings on corticosteroids in septic shock?

options.A: Both trials showed reduced 90-day mortality with hydrocortisone, with or without fludrocortisone
options.B: APROCCHSS showed increased superinfection and mortality with combined corticosteroid therapy
options.C: ADRENAL showed increased mortality with hydrocortisone
options.D: APROCCHSS (with fludrocortisone) reduced 90-day mortality; ADRENAL (hydrocortisone alone) did not
options.E: Neither trial showed faster shock reversal

explanation: ADRENAL (3800 patients; hydrocortisone 200 mg/day infusion) showed no mortality difference but faster shock reversal and fewer transfusions. APROCCHSS (hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours plus fludrocortisone 50 µg) showed lower 90-day mortality (43% vs 49.1%). Both reduced vasopressor duration.
referenceText: Venkatesh et al. 2018 (ADRENAL) [225]; Annane et al. 2018 (APROCCHSS) [10]

stem: What is the current evidence regarding intravenous vitamin C in sepsis?

options.A: It shortens vasopressor duration without harm
options.B: LOVIT found more death or persistent organ dysfunction, and SSC advises against its use
options.C: It is recommended only in patients with lactate above 4 mmol/L
options.D: It reduces mortality by about 50% when combined with thiamine and hydrocortisone (HAT therapy)
options.E: It is recommended for all patients with septic shock

explanation: LOVIT randomised 872 ICU patients with sepsis on vasopressors and found a higher composite of death or persistent organ dysfunction at 28 days with vitamin C. VITAMINS and other trials found no benefit of combination therapy. SSC 2021 suggests against its use. SSC 2026 suggests against IV vitamin C (conditional, low certainty).
referenceText: Lamontagne et al. 2022 (LOVIT) [123]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: Which patient with septic shock should receive empirical anti-MRSA coverage according to SSC 2021?

options.A: All patients with septic shock regardless of risk
options.B: Patients with biliary sepsis from gallstones
options.C: A patient at high MRSA risk, such as prior MRSA infection or colonisation
options.D: Patients with community-acquired urinary tract infection without risk factors
options.E: No patient; MRSA coverage should await culture results

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends empirical MRSA coverage for patients with sepsis or septic shock at high risk of MRSA (prior infection or colonisation, recent IV antibiotics, recurrent skin infections, haemodialysis, high local prevalence), and against coverage in low-risk patients.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]

stem: A patient with septic shock from hospital-acquired pneumonia in an ICU with high rates of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria needs empirical therapy. What does SSC 2021 suggest?

options.A: Two Gram-negative agents empirically, de-escalating once susceptibilities are known
options.B: No Gram-negative coverage until cultures and susceptibilities return
options.C: A single narrow-spectrum penicillin
options.D: Three Gram-negative agents for at least 14 days, regardless of culture and susceptibility results
options.E: An aminoglycoside alone

explanation: For patients at high risk of multidrug-resistant organisms, SSC 2021 suggests using two antimicrobials with Gram-negative coverage empirically, then discontinuing the second agent once the pathogen and susceptibilities are known. Routine double coverage is not suggested for low-risk patients. SSC 2026 suggests empirical multidrug-resistant coverage for patients at high risk and against it for low-risk patients (conditional, very low certainty), and recommends de-escalation once a confirmed microbiological diagnosis and susceptibilities are available (strong, very low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026 MDR coverage and de-escalation statements.

stem: How does SSC 2026 recommend administering beta-lactams for maintenance therapy in septic shock?

options.A: By oral route once haemodynamically stable on day 1
options.B: By prolonged infusion after an initial bolus
options.C: By intermittent bolus only every 24 hours
options.D: By continuous infusion without a loading dose
options.E: By intramuscular injection

explanation: Beta-lactams exhibit time-dependent killing; prolonged or continuous infusion increases the time that free drug concentration exceeds the MIC. SSC 2026 now recommends prolonged infusion of beta-lactams for maintenance after an initial loading dose over intermittent bolus administration (strong recommendation, moderate certainty), upgraded from a weak suggestion in SSC 2021. BLING III showed a non-significant reduction in 90-day mortality, with meta-analyses favouring continuous infusion.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Dulhunty et al. 2024 (BLING III) [56]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026: prolonged beta-lactam infusion upgraded to a strong recommendation.

stem: A patient's septic shock from pneumonia has resolved after 5 days of antibiotics. Procalcitonin has fallen by more than 80% from peak. How does SSC 2021 suggest procalcitonin be used?

options.A: Together with clinical evaluation to decide when to discontinue antimicrobials
options.B: To decide on source control surgery
options.C: To diagnose fungal infections
options.D: Procalcitonin is not recommended in any setting
options.E: To decide when to start antimicrobials in suspected septic shock, before cultures are taken

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests using procalcitonin with clinical evaluation to decide when to stop antimicrobials when the optimal duration is unclear, and recommends against using it to decide whether to start antibiotics. Shorter courses are suggested when adequate source control has been achieved. SSC 2026 retains procalcitonin plus clinical evaluation for discontinuation when duration is unclear (conditional, low certainty) and suggests against using it to start antibiotics.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with septic shock has a CT showing an infected obstructed left kidney with hydronephrosis and a stone. What is the most important intervention after starting antibiotics and resuscitation?

options.A: Renal biopsy
options.B: Diuretics to flush the collecting system and relieve the obstruction
options.C: Elective lithotripsy after 6 weeks
options.D: Antibiotics alone for 14 days
options.E: Urgent decompression by nephrostomy or ureteric stent

explanation: An obstructed infected kidney is a urological emergency requiring urgent decompression; antibiotics alone fail because of poor penetration and ongoing obstruction. SSC 2021 recommends rapidly identifying or excluding an anatomical source requiring control, with intervention as soon as medically and logistically practical. SSC 2026 suggests early over late source control, ideally within 6 hours (conditional, very low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient in septic shock has a central venous catheter inserted 10 days ago with purulence at the exit site. What should be done regarding the catheter?

options.A: Leave it in place and use antibiotic lock therapy
options.B: Exchange it over a guidewire at the same site
options.C: Remove it promptly after establishing other vascular access
options.D: Remove it only if blood cultures are positive at 72 hours
options.E: Flush with ethanol and continue using it

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends prompt removal of intravascular access devices that are a possible source of sepsis or septic shock, after other vascular access has been established. Guidewire exchange is inappropriate when the catheter is infected, particularly with exit-site infection.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Buetti et al. 2022 (SHEA/IDSA/APIC CLABSI prevention) [28]

stem: A patient with septic shock has pH 7.15, HCO3− 10 mmol/L, lactate 8 mmol/L and KDIGO stage 2 acute kidney injury. What does SSC 2021 suggest regarding sodium bicarbonate?

options.A: Bicarbonate is contraindicated in septic shock
options.B: Bicarbonate should be given to correct pH to 7.40 within 1 hour
options.C: Sodium bicarbonate is suggested, because pH is ≤7.2 with AKI stage 2 or 3
options.D: Tris-hydroxymethyl aminomethane must be used instead
options.E: Sodium bicarbonate is recommended in all patients with lactate above 4 mmol/L

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests against bicarbonate for hypoperfusion-induced lactic acidaemia in general, but suggests it for patients with pH ≤7.2 and AKIN stage 2 or 3, based on BICAR-ICU, which showed lower mortality and less need for renal replacement therapy in that subgroup. SSC 2026 retains this suggestion (conditional, very low certainty) and suggests against bicarbonate to improve haemodynamics or reduce vasopressor need.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Jaber et al. 2018 (BICAR-ICU) [102]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: What red-cell transfusion threshold is recommended for a patient with septic shock without myocardial ischaemia or acute haemorrhage?

options.A: Haemoglobin below 9 g/dL
options.B: Haemoglobin below 7 g/dL
options.C: Haemoglobin below 10 g/dL
options.D: Any fall in haemoglobin over 1 g/dL in 24 hours
options.E: Haematocrit below 30%

explanation: TRISS showed similar 90-day mortality and fewer transfusions with a threshold of 7 g/dL versus 9 g/dL in septic shock. SSC 2021 recommends a restrictive strategy (transfuse when haemoglobin is below 7 g/dL) for most adults. SSC 2026 recommends a restrictive over a liberal transfusion strategy (strong, moderate certainty).
referenceText: Holst et al. 2014 (TRISS) [94]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: Which adjunctive therapy is suggested against by SSC 2021 for adults with sepsis or septic shock?

options.A: Early enteral nutrition
options.B: Pharmacological VTE prophylaxis
options.C: Intravenous immunoglobulin
options.D: Stress ulcer prophylaxis in patients with bleeding risk factors
options.E: Insulin for glucose ≥10 mmol/L

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests against IV immunoglobulin and polymyxin B haemoperfusion in sepsis. It recommends VTE prophylaxis (preferably LMWH), suggests stress ulcer prophylaxis in patients with risk factors for GI bleeding, early enteral feeding and insulin for glucose of 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) or more. SSC 2026 again suggests against IV immunoglobulin and polymyxin B haemoperfusion (conditional, low certainty) and suggests proton pump inhibitors for patients with GI bleeding risk factors.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient in septic shock has a blood glucose of 12.5 mmol/L (225 mg/dL). What is the recommended management?

options.A: Start insulin, targeting 8–10 mmol/L (144–180 mg/dL)
options.B: Give oral metformin
options.C: No treatment unless glucose exceeds 20 mmol/L
options.D: Start insulin, targeting 4.4–6.1 mmol/L (80–110 mg/dL)
options.E: Stop all enteral feeding

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends initiating insulin at glucose ≥10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) with a typical target of 8–10 mmol/L. NICE-SUGAR showed higher mortality and severe hypoglycaemia with intensive targets of 4.5–6 mmol/L. SSC 2026 recommends starting insulin at glucose ≥10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) (strong, moderate certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; NICE-SUGAR Investigators 2009 [152]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: Which VTE prophylaxis is recommended for adults with sepsis without contraindications?

options.A: Low-molecular-weight heparin rather than unfractionated heparin
options.B: Therapeutic-dose heparin infusion
options.C: No prophylaxis because of DIC risk
options.D: Mechanical compression devices alone in all patients with sepsis
options.E: Aspirin 75 mg daily

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends pharmacological VTE prophylaxis and suggests LMWH over unfractionated heparin. It suggests against adding mechanical prophylaxis when pharmacological prophylaxis is used; mechanical methods are used when anticoagulants are contraindicated. SSC 2026 recommends pharmacological prophylaxis and LMWH over unfractionated heparin (strong, moderate certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Kahn et al. 2012 (ACCP VTE prevention, non-surgical) [108]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A diabetic man has rapidly spreading erythema, severe pain out of proportion, crepitus and bullae over the thigh with septic shock. What is the most important definitive intervention?

options.A: Needle aspiration of the bullae
options.B: Intravenous antibiotics alone for 48 hours, then reassess
options.C: Urgent surgical exploration and debridement
options.D: MRI of the thigh before any surgery
options.E: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as primary treatment

explanation: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency; mortality rises with delay. Management is early broad-spectrum antibiotics (including clindamycin for toxin suppression), resuscitation and urgent radical debridement with repeat explorations. Imaging must not delay surgery.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A young woman develops fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension and multiorgan dysfunction 3 days after nasal packing. Besides removal of the packing, which antibiotic combination is most appropriate?

options.A: Gentamicin alone
options.B: Metronidazole plus fluconazole for mixed anaerobic and fungal cover
options.C: Doxycycline alone
options.D: Ciprofloxacin alone
options.E: A beta-lactam (or vancomycin if MRSA risk) plus clindamycin

explanation: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome is toxin mediated. Clindamycin (or linezolid) inhibits protein and toxin synthesis and is added to a bactericidal agent (antistaphylococcal beta-lactam or vancomycin). IV immunoglobulin may be considered in severe streptococcal toxic shock.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Marino 2014 (The ICU Book, 4th ed.) [131]

stem: A 19-year-old student has fever, hypotension and a rapidly spreading purpuric rash. What is the most appropriate immediate antibiotic?

options.A: Wait for lumbar puncture results
options.B: Oral amoxicillin
options.C: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV without delay
options.D: Azithromycin
options.E: Vancomycin alone

explanation: Purpura fulminans with shock suggests meningococcal septicaemia, which requires immediate parenteral third-generation cephalosporin. Lumbar puncture is contraindicated with shock or coagulopathy and must not delay antibiotics. Close contacts require chemoprophylaxis.
referenceText: van de Beek et al. 2016 (ESCMID bacterial meningitis) [222]

stem: A patient who had a splenectomy after trauma 5 years ago presents with fever, hypotension and DIC. Which organism is most likely responsible?

options.A: Candida albicans
options.B: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.D: Mycoplasma pneumoniae
options.E: Clostridioides difficile

explanation: Overwhelming post-splenectomy infection is most commonly caused by encapsulated organisms, especially Streptococcus pneumoniae, followed by Haemophilus influenzae and Neisseria meningitidis. It progresses rapidly with high mortality; vaccination and early antibiotics are key.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Metlay et al. 2019 (ATS/IDSA community-acquired pneumonia) [138]

stem: A patient on chemotherapy with neutrophils 0.2 × 10⁹/L presents with fever and hypotension. What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.A: Oral ciprofloxacin plus amoxicillin–clavulanate, as used for low-risk outpatients with febrile neutropenia
options.B: Ceftriaxone alone
options.C: Vancomycin alone
options.D: An antipseudomonal beta-lactam (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam), adding agents for shock or resistance
options.E: Empirical fluconazole only

explanation: Febrile neutropenia requires prompt empirical antipseudomonal beta-lactam therapy (cefepime, piperacillin–tazobactam or a carbapenem). In septic shock, Gram-positive (vancomycin) and additional Gram-negative coverage are added. Oral therapy is only for low-risk outpatients.
referenceText: Freifeld et al. 2011 (IDSA febrile neutropenia) [71]

stem: A patient with gallstones has fever, jaundice, hypotension and dilated common bile duct on ultrasound. After antibiotics and resuscitation, what is the definitive source control?

options.A: Antibiotics alone for 6 weeks
options.B: Ursodeoxycholic acid
options.C: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 1 hour
options.D: Urgent biliary drainage, preferably by ERCP
options.E: Percutaneous liver biopsy

explanation: Acute cholangitis with septic shock requires urgent biliary decompression, preferably endoscopic (ERCP with sphincterotomy or stent); percutaneous transhepatic drainage is an alternative. Cholecystectomy is deferred until recovery. SSC 2026 suggests early over late source control, ideally within 6 hours.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A malnourished patient with alcohol use disorder in septic shock has persistently high lactate despite normal capillary refill, ScvO2 76% and normal cardiac output. What should be given?

options.A: More crystalloid to target lactate below 2 mmol/L
options.B: Dobutamine infusion
options.C: Sodium bicarbonate
options.D: Methylene blue
options.E: Intravenous thiamine

explanation: Thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase; deficiency shunts pyruvate to lactate, causing type B lactic acidosis. Patients with alcohol misuse, malnutrition or prolonged vomiting are at risk. Thiamine should be given before glucose and is safe.
referenceText: Kraut & Madias 2010 (metabolic acidosis) [120]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: Which statement about sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy is correct?

options.A: It is associated with permanent heart failure in most survivors
options.B: It always presents with regional wall motion abnormalities in a coronary distribution
options.C: It never affects the right ventricle
options.D: It is usually reversible within days to weeks in survivors
options.E: It requires urgent coronary angiography

explanation: Septic cardiomyopathy causes reversible biventricular systolic and/or diastolic dysfunction, often with dilated ventricles. Function typically recovers within 7–10 days in survivors. It is caused by inflammatory mediators, nitric oxide and mitochondrial dysfunction rather than coronary occlusion.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: What did the ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe trials and their patient-level meta-analysis (PRISM) show regarding early goal-directed therapy (EGDT) in septic shock?

options.A: EGDT did not reduce mortality and increased resource use compared with usual care
options.B: EGDT was beneficial only in patients with lactate above 4 mmol/L
options.C: EGDT reduced mortality by about 16%
options.D: EGDT reduced ICU admission
options.E: EGDT increased mortality significantly

explanation: In contrast to the single-centre Rivers trial, the three multicentre trials and PRISM meta-analysis found that protocolised EGDT (targeting CVP, ScvO2) did not improve survival and increased ICU admission and costs. SSC 2021 does not recommend CVP or ScvO2 targets. SSC 2026 suggests dynamic measures of fluid responsiveness over physical examination or static measures alone (conditional, low certainty).
referenceText: PRISM Investigators 2017 (early goal-directed therapy meta-analysis) [170]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: How should a fluid challenge be performed in a patient with septic shock beyond the initial resuscitation phase?

options.A: Fluid challenges should not be performed beyond the first 6 hours of resuscitation in septic shock
options.B: A defined volume (e.g. 250–500 mL) given rapidly, with a predefined endpoint and safety limits
options.C: Continuous infusion of 200 mL/h until urine output improves above 0.5 mL/kg/h
options.D: Albumin 20% only
options.E: 2 L bolus over 30 minutes in all patients

explanation: A fluid challenge consists of a small, rapid volume with assessment of response (e.g. stroke volume or cardiac output increase of at least 10–15%) and safety limits such as rising CVP or deteriorating oxygenation. It tests preload responsiveness while limiting cumulative fluid overload. SSC 2026 suggests guiding further fluids with dynamic measures such as passive leg raising or response to a fluid bolus (conditional, low certainty).
referenceText: Cecconi et al. 2014 (ESICM shock consensus) [34]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with sepsis from intra-abdominal infection had adequate source control by laparotomy and is clinically improving. What does SSC 2021 suggest regarding treatment duration?

options.A: Continue antibiotics until all surgical drains are removed, regardless of the clinical state
options.B: Continue antibiotics until CRP is normal
options.C: At least 21 days of IV therapy
options.D: Two weeks of carbapenem regardless of culture results
options.E: A shorter rather than longer course, with daily reassessment for de-escalation

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests shorter over longer antimicrobial durations for adults with sepsis and adequate source control, and daily assessment for de-escalation. In the STOP-IT trial, about 4 days of antibiotics after source control in intra-abdominal infection was as effective as longer courses. SSC 2026 retains shorter courses with adequate source control (conditional, very low certainty) and recommends de-escalation once susceptibilities are known (strong, very low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with septic shock has a history of a rash with penicillin 20 years ago. Which antibiotic decision is most appropriate?

options.A: Perform penicillin skin testing before any beta-lactam antibiotic is given
options.B: Use aztreonam monotherapy for all infections, including suspected Gram-positive sepsis
options.C: Use a cephalosporin or carbapenem; cross-reactivity is low after a mild remote rash
options.D: All beta-lactams are absolutely contraindicated
options.E: Give no Gram-negative coverage

explanation: Most reported penicillin allergies are not true IgE-mediated allergies, and cross-reactivity with cephalosporins (especially those with different side chains) and carbapenems is about 1–2%. Delaying effective therapy in septic shock for allergy assessment increases mortality.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

stem: Which mechanism contributes most to vasodilation and vasopressor hyporesponsiveness in septic shock?

options.A: Inducible NO synthase overproduction, K-ATP channel activation and vasopressin deficiency
options.B: Increased angiotensin II sensitivity
options.C: Primary myocardial infarction
options.D: Increased blood viscosity
options.E: Upregulated adrenergic receptor density and enhanced vascular calcium sensitivity

explanation: Septic vasoplegia results from inducible nitric oxide synthase, opening of K-ATP channels, adrenergic receptor downregulation, relative vasopressin deficiency, corticosteroid insufficiency and glycocalyx damage. These mechanisms underlie therapies such as vasopressin, corticosteroids and methylene blue.
referenceText: Singer et al. 2016 (Sepsis-3) [198]; Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]

stem: A patient with septic shock after abdominal surgery has total parenteral nutrition, a central line, broad-spectrum antibiotics for 10 days and Candida colonisation at multiple sites. Which approach is most appropriate according to SSC 2026?

options.A: No antifungal therapy until biopsy confirms invasive disease
options.B: Amphotericin B only after blood cultures remain positive for Candida for 2 weeks
options.C: Fluconazole in all patients with sepsis
options.D: Antifungal therapy only if the patient is neutropenic
options.E: Empirical antifungal therapy such as an echinocandin, given the high fungal risk

explanation: SSC 2026 suggests against routine empirical antifungal therapy in adults with sepsis or septic shock (conditional, low certainty), but advises considering it case by case in selected patients with fungal risk factors, as here. Risk factors include abdominal surgery, TPN, central lines, broad-spectrum antibiotics, multifocal colonisation and renal replacement therapy. Echinocandins are preferred initially for critically ill patients.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Pappas et al. 2016 (IDSA candidiasis) [161]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026: against routine empirical antifungals; case-by-case use in high-risk patients.

stem: Which is a recognised long-term consequence of sepsis in survivors?

options.A: Improved quality of life compared with baseline
options.B: New cognitive impairment, disability and more rehospitalisation
options.C: Complete recovery within 1 month in all survivors
options.D: Lifelong immunity to further infection
options.E: Permanent dialysis dependence in most survivors after hospital discharge

explanation: Sepsis survivors have increased risks of cognitive impairment, physical disability, psychological morbidity, recurrent infection, cardiovascular events and rehospitalisation. SSC 2021 recommends screening for these problems, follow-up and rehabilitation.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Needham et al. 2012 (post-intensive care syndrome) [150]

stem: For a patient with septic shock and poor prognosis, what does SSC 2021 recommend about discussing goals of care?

options.A: Leave decisions to the admitting surgeon alone
options.B: Discuss goals of care and prognosis early, ideally within 72 hours of ICU admission
options.C: Avoid goals-of-care discussions until the patient recovers
options.D: Goals of care should be discussed only if the family specifically requests such a meeting
options.E: Discuss only after 2 weeks of ICU treatment

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends that goals of care and prognosis be discussed with patients and families, and suggests addressing them early (within 72 hours) rather than late. Palliative care principles should be incorporated where appropriate.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Truog et al. 2008 (ACCM end-of-life care) [216]

stem: A patient in septic shock has blood cultures growing ceftriaxone-resistant Escherichia coli (ESBL producer). What is the preferred definitive therapy?

options.A: A carbapenem such as meropenem
options.B: Cefazolin
options.C: Amoxicillin–clavulanate
options.D: Ceftriaxone at high dose
options.E: Piperacillin–tazobactam as definitive therapy

explanation: IDSA guidance recommends carbapenems for serious infections caused by ESBL-producing Enterobacterales outside the urinary tract. The MERINO trial showed higher mortality with piperacillin–tazobactam compared with meropenem for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli or Klebsiella bacteraemia. SSC 2026 recommends de-escalation once a confirmed microbiological diagnosis and susceptibility profile are available (strong, very low certainty).
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with septic shock has bloodstream infection with KPC-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which antibiotic is a preferred option?

options.A: Ceftazidime–avibactam
options.B: Colistin monotherapy as first choice
options.C: Ampicillin–sulbactam
options.D: Ceftriaxone
options.E: Meropenem monotherapy

explanation: IDSA guidance prefers newer beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitors such as ceftazidime–avibactam, meropenem–vaborbactam or imipenem–relebactam for KPC-producing Enterobacterales. Polymyxins are less effective and more toxic. For metallo-beta-lactamase producers (e.g. NDM), ceftazidime–avibactam plus aztreonam or cefiderocol is preferred.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

stem: A patient with septic shock has bacteraemia with NDM (metallo-beta-lactamase)-producing Klebsiella pneumoniae. Which regimen is preferred?

options.A: Meropenem–vaborbactam
options.B: Imipenem–relebactam
options.C: Ertapenem plus meropenem
options.D: Ceftazidime–avibactam alone as an extended infusion
options.E: Ceftazidime–avibactam plus aztreonam, or cefiderocol

explanation: Metallo-beta-lactamases (NDM, VIM, IMP) are not inhibited by avibactam, vaborbactam or relebactam. Aztreonam is stable to MBL hydrolysis but is inactivated by co-produced serine beta-lactamases, which avibactam inhibits. Hence ceftazidime–avibactam plus aztreonam, or cefiderocol, is preferred.
referenceText: Tamma et al. 2024 (IDSA resistant Gram-negative guidance) [205]

stem: Which statement about fever control in septic patients is correct?

options.A: Antipyretics improve bacterial clearance
options.B: Fever is harmful in all cases and should always be treated with NSAIDs
options.C: Paracetamol reduces 90-day mortality in sepsis
options.D: Routine antipyresis to normothermia has not been shown to improve survival
options.E: Fever must always be reduced below 37 °C, using external cooling devices if antipyretics fail

explanation: Trials such as HEAT (paracetamol in febrile ICU patients with infection) showed no effect on ICU-free days or mortality. Fever may be treated for comfort or in patients with limited cardiopulmonary reserve or brain injury, but routine aggressive control is not recommended.
referenceText: Bersten & Handy 2019 (Oh's Intensive Care Manual, 8th ed.) [18]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]

stem: For an adult with septic shock who can be fed enterally, what nutritional approach does SSC 2021 suggest?

options.A: Nil by mouth for 7 days
options.B: High-protein parenteral feeding in addition to enteral feeding
options.C: Omega-3 supplementation as immune nutrition
options.D: Early parenteral nutrition within 24 hours in all patients
options.E: Early enteral feeding (within 72 hours)

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests starting early enteral nutrition (within 72 hours) in adults with sepsis who can be fed enterally, and suggests against omega-3 supplementation as immunonutrition. Early parenteral nutrition is not superior and is associated with more infections in some trials. SSC 2026 retains early enteral nutrition within 72 hours (conditional, very low certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Singer et al. 2019 (ESPEN ICU nutrition) [199]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: Which septic patient should receive stress ulcer prophylaxis according to SSC 2021?

options.A: Only patients already taking NSAIDs at home
options.B: No patient, because proton pump inhibitors increase pneumonia and C. difficile
options.C: Every patient with sepsis, regardless of bleeding risk, for the whole ICU stay
options.D: Only patients receiving enteral nutrition
options.E: A patient with GI bleeding risk factors, such as coagulopathy, shock or chronic liver disease

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests stress ulcer prophylaxis for patients with sepsis who have risk factors for GI bleeding. SUP-ICU found no mortality difference with pantoprazole but fewer clinically important bleeding events. SSC 2026 suggests proton pump inhibitors for patients with risk factors for GI bleeding (conditional, moderate certainty).
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; Krag et al. 2018 (SUP-ICU) [119]; Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with pneumonia has new confusion (GCS 13), PaO2/FiO2 of 250 mmHg on face-mask oxygen, bilirubin normal, creatinine 180 µmol/L (2.0 mg/dL) and MAP 70 mmHg without vasopressors. Baseline SOFA was 0. What is the approximate SOFA score now?
explanation: SOFA points: CNS GCS 13–14 = 1; respiratory P/F below 300 = 2; renal creatinine 171–299 µmol/L (2.0–3.4 mg/dL) = 2; cardiovascular MAP ≥70 mmHg = 0; liver and coagulation 0. Total = 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, meeting the Sepsis-3 criterion of an increase of 2 or more. SOFA-2 note: a revised score, SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025), keeps six organ systems (renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis), updates the organ-support drugs and devices used for scoring, revises several thresholds and adds alternative variables when measurements are unavailable; it predicted ICU mortality slightly better (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.77). Sepsis-3 is defined with the original SOFA score, so this calculation uses the original SOFA.
referenceText: Singer et al. 2016 (Sepsis-3) [198]; Vincent et al. 1996 (SOFA score) [229]; SOFA-2, JAMA 2025 [250]
updateNote: SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025) note added; calculation uses original SOFA, as Sepsis-3 requires.

stem: A patient with septic shock has KDIGO stage 3 AKI but no hyperkalaemia, refractory acidosis, fluid overload or uraemic complications. What does SSC 2021 suggest regarding renal replacement therapy?

options.A: Do not start RRT solely for creatinine rise or oliguria without definitive indications
options.B: Start continuous RRT immediately
options.C: RRT should be started when urine output falls below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours
options.D: Use high-volume haemofiltration to remove cytokines
options.E: Start intermittent haemodialysis within 6 hours

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests against using RRT in patients with sepsis and AKI for increases in creatinine or oliguria without other definitive indications. STARRT-AKI found no survival benefit from accelerated RRT initiation and more RRT dependence at 90 days.
referenceText: Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]; STARRT-AKI Investigators 2020 [202]

stem: A patient with septic shock is started on gentamicin as part of empirical double Gram-negative coverage. Which dosing strategy best matches the pharmacodynamics of aminoglycosides?

options.A: Small doses every 4 hours to keep concentrations constant
options.B: A high once-daily dose (e.g. 5–7 mg/kg) to maximise peak/MIC, with trough monitoring
options.C: Dose reduction on day 1, because the volume of distribution is increased by capillary leak
options.D: Continuous infusion to maximise time above MIC
options.E: Oral administration once the patient is stable

explanation: Aminoglycosides exhibit concentration-dependent killing and a post-antibiotic effect, so efficacy depends on peak/MIC (target about 8–10). Sepsis increases volume of distribution, so a full loading dose is needed. Extended-interval dosing also reduces nephrotoxicity by allowing low troughs.
referenceText: Abdul-Aziz et al. 2020 (antimicrobial TDM position paper) [1]; Evans et al. 2021 (Surviving Sepsis Campaign) [65]

stem: A 58-year-old man with pneumonia has a baseline SOFA of 0. He now has platelets 90 × 10^9/L, bilirubin 1.4 mg/dL, MAP 68 mmHg without vasopressors, and GCS 14. How should this be classified under Sepsis-3?

options.A: Sepsis; SOFA has risen by ≥2 points due to infection
options.B: Septic shock; organ dysfunction with thrombocytopenia
options.C: SIRS only; sepsis requires a positive blood culture
options.D: Infection without sepsis; MAP is above 65 mmHg

explanation: SOFA: platelets 50–99 = 2, bilirubin 1.2–1.9 = 1, GCS 13–14 = 1 → rise of 4 from baseline. Sepsis-3 defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction (acute SOFA rise ≥2) caused by a dysregulated host response to infection. Strongest distractor: Septic shock additionally requires vasopressors for MAP ≥65 and lactate >2 mmol/L despite adequate fluids. SOFA-2 note: a revised score, SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025), keeps six organ systems (renamed brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis), updates the organ-support drugs and devices used for scoring, revises several thresholds and adds alternative variables when measurements are unavailable; it predicted ICU mortality slightly better (AUROC 0.79 vs 0.77). Sepsis-3 is defined with the original SOFA score, so this calculation uses the original SOFA.
referenceText: SOFA-2, JAMA 2025 [250]
updateNote: SOFA-2 (JAMA 2025) note added; calculation uses original SOFA, as Sepsis-3 requires.

stem: A 64-year-old woman has fever, confusion and BP 82/45 mmHg not responding to fluids, with a likely urinary source. When should antibiotics be given?

options.A: Within 6 hours, once urine culture is reported
options.B: Only after CT has confirmed the infection source
options.C: Within 3 hours, after full diagnostic work-up and imaging
options.D: Immediately, ideally within 1 hour of recognition

explanation: SSC 2026 recommends antimicrobials immediately, ideally within 1 hour, for septic shock and for probable or definite sepsis without shock (strong, very low certainty). For possible sepsis without shock it retains a time-limited approach: rapid assessment, with antimicrobials within 3 hours if concern persists. Strongest distractor: The 3-hour window applies to possible sepsis without shock.
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026 wording of the 1-hour antimicrobial recommendation.

stem: A septic patient's lactate is 4.2 mmol/L at hour 0. When should it be re-measured?

options.A: Within 2–4 hours to guide resuscitation
options.B: Only after 24 hours, when clearance is reliable
options.C: Not repeated, as one value is enough
options.D: Every 15 minutes until it normalises

explanation: SSC suggests remeasuring lactate (if initially elevated) to guide resuscitation, typically within 2–4 hours, as its kinetics are slow. Strongest distractor: Very frequent sampling adds little because lactate falls slowly. SSC 2026 suggests serial lactate measurement to guide resuscitation (conditional, low certainty), with fluids individualised after the initial bolus rather than aiming to normalise lactate.
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A nursing-home resident with septic shock from pneumonia had MRSA isolated from sputum 3 months ago. What empirical cover is recommended?

options.A: Add antifungal cover instead of MRSA cover
options.B: Add MRSA cover (e.g. vancomycin or linezolid)
options.C: No MRSA cover until cultures are reported
options.D: Add MRSA cover only if Gram stain shows cocci

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends empirical MRSA coverage for adults with sepsis or septic shock at high risk of MRSA (prior MRSA colonisation or infection, recent IV antibiotics). Strongest distractor: Delaying MRSA cover in a high-risk patient with shock risks inadequate initial therapy. SSC 2026 likewise suggests empirical coverage for multidrug-resistant organisms in patients at high risk, and against it for low-risk patients (conditional, very low certainty).
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with septic shock from an infected necrotic gallbladder is stabilising on noradrenaline. When should source control be done?

options.A: After repeat imaging confirms the source at 48 hours
options.B: As soon as medically and logistically practical
options.C: After 72 hours of antibiotics to sterilise the source
options.D: Only when vasopressors have been weaned off

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends rapid identification and implementation of source control as soon as practical (best-practice statement). Strongest distractor: Waiting for haemodynamic stability may never be achieved without source control. SSC 2026 suggests early over late source control, ideally within 6 hours (conditional, very low certainty).
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A patient with septic shock has lactic acidosis, pH 7.24, and no AKI. Should sodium bicarbonate be given?

options.A: No; bicarbonate is not suggested for pH ≥7.2 from hypoperfusion
options.B: Yes; it improves haemodynamics at any pH below 7.35
options.C: Yes; it reduces vasopressor requirements in all patients
options.D: No; bicarbonate is harmful even in patients with AKI and pH ≤7.2

explanation: SSC 2021 suggests against bicarbonate for hypoperfusion-induced lactic acidaemia with pH ≥7.2, and suggests it for pH ≤7.2 with AKIN 2–3 (BICAR-ICU subgroup benefit). Strongest distractor: BICAR-ICU showed benefit in the AKI subgroup, so it is not universally harmful. SSC 2026 retains this suggestion (conditional, very low certainty) and suggests against bicarbonate to improve haemodynamics or reduce vasopressor need.
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: A stable septic patient without ischaemia has Hb 7.6 g/dL. What is the transfusion threshold?

options.A: Transfuse now to keep Hb above 10 g/dL
options.B: Transfuse now to keep Hb above 9 g/dL
options.C: Transfuse at Hb <7 g/dL (restrictive strategy)
options.D: Transfuse only if ScvO2 is below 70%

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends a restrictive transfusion strategy (Hb 7 g/dL); TRISS showed no difference in mortality between 7 and 9 g/dL thresholds. Strongest distractor: Hb 9 g/dL (TRISS liberal arm) doubled transfusions without benefit. SSC 2026 recommends a restrictive over a liberal transfusion strategy (strong, moderate certainty).
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: What VTE prophylaxis is recommended for a septic patient without contraindication?

options.A: No prophylaxis until the patient is mobilising
options.B: Pharmacological prophylaxis, preferably LMWH over UFH
options.C: Mechanical plus pharmacological prophylaxis for all
options.D: Mechanical prophylaxis alone with compression devices

explanation: SSC 2021 recommends pharmacological VTE prophylaxis, LMWH preferred over UFH, and suggests against adding mechanical prophylaxis routinely. Strongest distractor: Combined mechanical plus pharmacological prophylaxis gave no added benefit (PREVENT). SSC 2026 recommends pharmacological prophylaxis and LMWH over unfractionated heparin (strong, moderate certainty).
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]

stem: Lactate falls from 6.0 to 4.2 mmol/L over 2 hours. What is the lactate clearance?
explanation: Clearance = (6.0 − 4.2) / 6.0 × 100 = 30%. Lactate clearance ≥10–20% early is associated with better outcomes, but lactate must be interpreted with perfusion markers. Strongest distractor: 43% divides by the final value (1.8/4.2) instead of the initial value.

stem: A 25-year-old woman has fever, diffuse erythroderma, hypotension and multiorgan failure; a tampon was in place. Which antibiotic should be added to beta-lactam therapy?

options.A: Azithromycin, to cover atypical organisms
options.B: Metronidazole, to cover anaerobes
options.C: Clindamycin, to suppress toxin production
options.D: Gentamicin, to double Gram-negative cover

explanation: Toxic shock syndrome (staphylococcal or streptococcal): remove the source, give a beta-lactam (± vancomycin) plus clindamycin (or linezolid) to inhibit toxin synthesis; consider IVIG in streptococcal TSS. Strongest distractor: Gentamicin has no anti-toxin effect.

stem: Should empirical antifungal therapy be routinely added in septic shock?

options.A: Only in patients at high risk of fungal infection
options.B: Never, until cultures grow yeast
options.C: Yes, in all patients with septic shock on vasopressors
options.D: Only if the platelet count falls below 50

explanation: SSC 2026 suggests against routine empirical antifungal therapy in adults with sepsis or septic shock (conditional, low certainty), and advises considering it case by case in patients with fungal risk factors (e.g. neutropenia, TPN, recent abdominal surgery, Candida colonisation at multiple sites). Strongest distractor: Routine empirical antifungals increase resistance and cost.
referenceText: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 [248]
updateNote: SSC 2026: against routine empirical antifungals; case-by-case use in high-risk patients.
